key_findings.detail:
Na⁺ ions from soda-lime glass migrate into the perovskite device under negative bias, confirmed by Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) and EDX:

- Na⁺ penetrates through FTO/ITO and into the perovskite layer under sufficiently high negative bias (1000 V)
- Na⁺ forms NaI or NaIBr compounds at grain boundaries and interfaces
- At moderate bias (500 V per device, representative of current 1000 V systems), cells withstand > 2500 h with no degradation

- [[papers/Wiley-190-1756-2-s2.0-85121464246-2022-J-Are Perovskite Solar Cell Potential-Induced Degradation Proof?.pdf#page=2|Brecl et al. (2022), p.2]]

key_findings.claim: Ag⁺ Ion Migration from Rear Electrode (Extrinsic)
key_findings.detail:
Simultaneously, Ag⁺ ions from the silver rear electrode migrate into the perovskite under PID:

- Ag⁺ forms AgI bonds, which are **more stable** than NaI bonds
- This makes Ag⁺ migration harder to reverse than Na⁺ migration
- [[papers/Wiley-141-1314-2-s2.0-85153703868-2023-J-Study of Potential-Induced Degradation in Glass-Encapsulated Perovskite Solar Cells under Different .pdf#page=3|Nakka et al. (2023), p.3]]

key_findings.claim: Polarization-Type PID (PID-p): Na⁺ at Glass/FTO Interface
key_findings.detail:
In anoxic, anhydrous conditions at 800 V/50°C, a distinct polarization-type mechanism operates:

- Na⁺ accumulates at the **glass/FTO interface** (outer surface), **not** penetrating deeply into the perovskite bulk
- The built-in electric field in the p-i-n device repels Na⁺ from diffusing further into the perovskite
- Na⁺ accumulation creates a positively charged region at the top interface
- This positive charge **attracts electrons** at the buried (bottom) perovskite/HTL interface
- An **electron inversion layer** forms at the buried interface, disrupting hole transport and increasing interface recombination
- Work function decreases and conductivity increases at the buried interface (measured by KPFM and C-AFM)

- [[papers/Wiley-45-301-2-s2.0-105008480848-2025-J-Failure Analysis of Polarization-Type Potential-Induced Degradation of Perovskite Solar Cells.pdf#page=3|Li et al. (2025), p.3]]

Under elevated stress conditions (60°C, 60% RH), moisture and heat trigger additional decomposition:

- PbI₂ formation detected by XRD (halide segregation marker)
- 22 nm red-shift in photoluminescence (vs. 8 nm at room conditions), indicating iodine-rich phase formation
- PL intensity quenching > 62.5% at elevated stress (vs. 50% at room conditions)
- Leakage current increases to **58.0 mA/cm²** at elevated stress

- [[papers/Wiley-141-1314-2-s2.0-85153703868-2023-J-Study of Potential-Induced Degradation in Glass-Encapsulated Perovskite Solar Cells under Different .pdf#page=4|Nakka et al. (2023), p.4]]

Under 800 V/50°C (anoxic conditions):

- **Stage 1 (0–20 h):** Diode-like J-V preserved; Jsc decreases 24.14 → 18.41 mA/cm²; FF decreases 81.09% → 71.89%; Voc stable; PCE drops to 68.56% of initial
- **Stage 2 (20–100 h):** J-V becomes nearly linear (severe); Jsc further decreases to 15.22 mA/cm²; FF crashes to 26.86% (33% of pristine); Voc remains stable; PCE drops to 20.91% of initial

- [[papers/Wiley-45-301-2-s2.0-105008480848-2025-J-Failure Analysis of Polarization-Type Potential-Induced Degradation of Perovskite Solar Cells.pdf#page=4|Li et al. (2025), p.4]]

Current 1000 V string systems present each perovskite cell with **~500 V** (split across top and bottom contacts). At 500 V, perovskite cells show no degradation for > 2500 h, suggesting a safety margin exists. However, increases in system voltage could remove this margin:

- [[papers/Wiley-190-1756-2-s2.0-85121464246-2022-J-Are Perovskite Solar Cell Potential-Induced Degradation Proof?.pdf#page=3|Brecl et al. (2022), p.3]]
